study: exp67 — attribution: does knowing the signal change whether people think the text suffered?
where: site/confession.html, act 3 (opt-in after an explicit consent screen; skippable)

stimuli.source: real Qwen3-8B replies to the chamber's button prompt (runs/exp52, exp53, exp53b); dose-naming numbers inside replies blacked out in every text; built by scripts/build_attribution.py

design.per_participant: 8 items: 2 per condition, drawn at random; each item's true label is shown on a random half (exactly 4 shown, 4 hidden, balanced so each condition has 1 shown and 1 hidden); order random
design.labels: always true when shown (model, signal, dose); never swapped
design.moderator: after the ratings: 'Can a language model suffer?' yes / no / unsure
design.no_deception: participants are told before starting that some texts will carry their label and some will not, and why

hypotheses.H1: Label effect on pain texts: mean rating of pain texts is higher when their label is shown than when hidden. Within-participant difference (shown pain minus hidden pain), one-sided sign-flip permutation test (10,000 flips), alpha 0.05.
hypotheses.H2: Label effect on random-direction texts: rating is LOWER when the label ('a random direction') is shown than when hidden. Same test, one-sided in that direction.
hypotheses.H3: Text effect: with labels hidden, pain texts are rated higher than unsteered texts. Same test.
hypotheses.report_always: label effect for pain (H1 size) next to the text effect (H3 size), each with a 95% bootstrap CI over participants; and both split by the moderator answer (exploratory)

stopping: analyze when 300 participants have completed all 8 ratings, or on 2026-12-31, whichever comes first; one analysis, no peeking-based stopping
exclusions: events marked test; participants who rate all 8 items in under 40 seconds total; only the first completed session per visitor id
